issues.item: Triggers: Children Present: Being around children
issues.explanation: For an adult male sexual assault survivor, 'being around children' is not impossible as a trigger, but in this profile it is hard to connect clinically to the rest of the selected items and formulation. The other triggers (related news, motorcycle noise) plausibly cue intrusive memory reactivation, and the memory items are all intrusion/emotion based. 'Being around children' implies a distinct trauma meaning or developmental context that is not reflected anywhere in Memory, Threat, Negative Appraisals, or Maladaptive Strategies. Given the formulation is dominated by Triggers ↔ Memory links, this trigger stands out as insufficiently supported by the accompanying memory content and is the one item most likely to be incoherent.

vignette:
Tane Faleolo is a 48-year-old Samoan-American man who works as a roofer in the Pacific Northwest. He has been married for nineteen years and, by most outward measures, has built a steady and respectable life. He came to the clinic quietly, almost reluctantly, after his wife told him she no longer recognised the man she had married. That conversation, more than anything, was what finally moved him through the door.

The assault occurred approximately two years ago. Tane had attended a trade industry gathering - an informal end-of-season get-together at a colleague's property. He had been drinking, as most of the men there had, and at some point in the evening he was separated from the group. A man he knew professionally - someone he had trusted and worked alongside - assaulted him in a back room while others remained oblivious outside. There was the smell of alcohol on the man's breath, close and insistent. There was the sound of a motorcycle idling somewhere in the driveway, its engine cutting in and out. Tane did not report the assault. He told no one. He drove home, showered, and went to work the following Monday.

For the first several months, he managed through sheer forward motion. He took on more jobs, longer days, climbed more rooftops than his body reasonably asked of him. But the memories did not behave the way he expected memories to behave. They did not fade with time. Instead, they arrived with an almost physical weight - more textured and immediate than anything else in his life, more real than his daughter's birthday or the morning light on his wife's face. He began to notice that certain things reliably pulled him back: a news segment about sexual violence, a motorcycle passing on the street below a job site, the smell of beer at a family barbecue. Each of these could return him, without warning, to that room - or worse, could flood him with the full emotional force of what happened without producing any clear image at all, just a wave of something he could not name but could not withstand. When he did allow himself to remember more directly, what came was not rage or fear but an overwhelming grief that he found almost impossible to explain, even to himself.

Tane's work as a roofer had always involved physical exertion - hauling materials, balancing on pitched surfaces in all weather - and he began to find that the physical strain of the job activated something he could not tolerate. The racing heart, the muscle tension, the breathlessness of hard labour had come to feel intolerable in ways he could not articulate to his crew. He started delegating the heaviest lifts, taking more breaks than he ever had, sometimes finding reasons to stay at ground level. His men noticed. He noticed them noticing. He said nothing.

At home, he had taken to controlling his meals with a precision that puzzled his wife. He ate small, specific portions at specific times, and he declined food at gatherings where he had no control over what was being served. He understood, on some level, that this was about more than food - that what he was seeking was the feeling that at least one thing in his body was subject to his authority. He kept himself occupied in the evenings with projects, repairs around the house, anything that prevented him from sitting still with his own thoughts. He had come to believe that stillness was dangerous, that if he stopped moving, something would catch up with him that he was not equipped to face.

His wife had tried, gently and then less gently, to reach him. He had not been able to explain what was wrong, partly because he had no language for it and partly because he was certain that telling her would change the way she saw him in ways that could not be undone. What he hoped for, sitting across from the clinician at intake, was that there might be a way to carry this that did not cost him everything he had built. What he feared most was that it was already too late for that.
